title: Multiplexed routing & KV-cache strategies for MoE + dense models (Llama/Mistral/Qwen) - deep dive
topics: MoE routing costs and token multiplexing
KV cache eviction policies and prefix caching
VPC/on-prem networking and private control plane
summary: Redwood SEs walked Vertex Labs through a performance plan for a hybrid workload mixing dense and MoE models. Main outcomes: agree to run three benchmark permutations (4k context dense, 8k with MoE routing, and cache-warm long-tail serving), test nf4 vs int8 on p4d-like instances, and validate VPC private control plane latency with their firewall/NAT setup. Action items assigned to run benchmarks and share config templates and security docs.
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-11-20
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Jon (Redwood Infra), Chris (Vertex ML Platform), Dina (Vertex Infra), Omar (Vertex Research)
Shared artifacts: benchmark-plan-vertex.xlsx, security-one-pager.pdf, kvcache-strategies.md (links in follow-up)

[00:00] Alex: Okay, hey everyone thanks for carving out the time, I know we had a fairly deep agenda, so we'll start with a quick context check, then Maya will take the technical walkthrough and Jon will cover infra implications.
[00:18] Chris: Yep, thanks Alex. High level we're trying to surface where inference cost is blowing up—our prod mix is like 70% dense (Llama-2-like), 30% MoE for high-cap tasks. We're seeing latency spikes when routing flares, and KV cache growth is... problematic.
[00:32] Maya: Great, that's exactly where we want to dig in. Quick clarifying Q: when you say 'KV cache growth'—is that per-request KV for long contexts, or are you seeing cross-request growth due to prefix caching?
[00:45] Omar: It's a bit of both. We have heavy few-shot prompts that build long prefix contexts, and some users keep long sessions which pushes our KVs in memory. We also get bursts where lots of unique prefixes reduce hit rate.
[01:02] Maya: Understood. So our recommendations split into three buckets: routing and batching strategies for MoE, KV-cache policies and prefix eviction, and quantization/kernel choices per model family. We'll run through live traces and a proposed benchmark matrix.
[01:20] Alex: Quick note—Dina, any blocking infra constraints for testing the private plane? You mentioned firewall/NAT timeouts in the doc.
[01:29] Dina: Yeah, our gateways close idle TCP after 30s which messes with long-lived control plane streams; we need to validate the private control plane's keepalive cadence. Also any UDP-based health checks will be blocked.
[01:41] Jon: That's useful. Redwood private control plane supports configurable keepalives; we can set it to 20s or 10s. For on-prem we recommend a TCP keepalive of 15s plus periodic session refresh to avoid NAT timeouts. We'll show how to configure it in the VPC template.
[01:57] Maya: Ok jumping into routing. For MoE models (we talked about the 64-expert and 128-expert configs), the routing cost is twofold: 1) the router compute and 2) downstream expert fanout which increases memory traffic and KV cache pressure if experts have different KV states. For token multiplexing strategies we suggest dispatching tokens in micro-batches grouped by routing hash to reduce expert fragmentation.
[02:28] Chris: Can you explain the 'routing hash' grouping—is that something Redwood runtime does automatically?
[02:32] Maya: Good question. We have two modes: default per-request routing (fast but causes scatter) and multiplexed routing where the runtime reorders in-flight tokens in short windows (20-50ms) to group tokens that route to the same expert. This trades a tiny additional latency (tail) for much better throughput and lower memory bandwidth because experts are fed denser batches.
[02:50] Omar: That sounds like continuous batching but with routing-aware grouping?
[02:55] Maya: Exactly. Continuous batching is across sequence positions and requests; multiplexed routing adds a routing-key stage that reorders tokens by the gating output. In practice we see 25-40% lower GPU memory copy overhead and up to 30% better throughput on MoE heavy workloads.
[03:10] Chris: Does it change token-level cost accounting? We need to reconcile billing when tokens get delayed/reordered.
[03:17] Alex: Internally we tag tokens for accounting—latency windows don't affect token counts, but if tokens get coalesced into larger micro-batches the per-token GPU time drops; we'll show a billing trace.
[03:25] Dina: Any implications for tail latency SLO? Our product SLO is p99 under 250ms.
[03:31] Maya: There's a tradeoff—if you want hard p99 under 250ms we can flip to low-latency mode where multiplexing windows are small (5-10ms) or disabled; cost rises. If you accept a soft p99 (e.g., median and 95 tight), multiplexed routing is much better. We'll provide config knobs and A/B thresholds.
[03:48] Jon: Also note that with persistent KV caches, if routing causes more cache misses (experts with cold caches), you see spikes. So we recommend two things: persistent per-expert KV shards anchored in GPU memory plus a local LRU eviction policy tuned to your session distribution.
[04:04] Omar: How big are these shards typically? We're using 2k tokens context in a few-shot flow but want to move to 8k for some use cases.
[04:12] Maya: For 8k you'd see KV sizes proportionally larger per request. We recommend capping per-session KV to a sliding window—keep the most recent 2k tokens in fast GPU LRU, and offload older prefixes to tenant-level SSD-backed cache with fast async prefetch when sessions reopen. That keeps hot-path latency low.
[04:29] Chris: How do you handle prefix similarity? We have many slightly-different prompts that share large prefixes. Can we canonicalize?
[04:36] Maya: Yes—prefix dedup is effective. We suggest a two-layer keying: canonicalize prompts with a fuzzy-hash (minhash or simhash) in the client library, then at runtime we perform exact prefix matching with a bloom filter to find shared KVs. It reduces duplicated KV storage and improves hit rate.
[04:50] Alex: On quantization—your prod mix uses Llama 2 13B dense and a custom MoE 24B. We tested nf4 on Mistral and int8 on Qwen?
[04:59] Omar: We have experimental int8 for Qwen but anxious about quality. We haven't tried nf4 at scale.
[05:05] Maya: Our internal benchmarks show nf4 is a sweet spot for many dense Mistral-family weights—low quality drop, high perf. For Qwen, int8 sometimes works but you need per-channel scale calibration and a fall back to int8+GPTQ-recenter for outlier layers. MoE is trickier: gating layers are sensitive to quantization; we only quantize expert FFNs, and often keep routing and gate layers in fp16.
[05:28] Dina: So we'd run a hybrid quant strategy: keep router and embedding fp16, quantize expert FFNs to nf4/int8?
[05:35] Maya: Exactly. And for MoE we recommend sparsity-aware kernels and fused router+dispatch kernels where possible. Redwood runtime will select those kernels if highway (NVFuser/Triton) kernels are available; otherwise we'll fall back to efficient CPU dispatch for routing.
[05:50] Chris: About RoPE/rope scaling—our models differ: Llama uses standard RoPE, Mistral has slightly different rotary base, and Qwen applies absolute positional mod. We're seeing context length degradation beyond 4k in some models.
[06:02] Maya: RoPE frequency scaling matters. For long contexts we can either rescale rotary frequencies (linear rescale or extrapolation), or use chunked attention with stateful KV stitching. Rescaling is lower overhead but can change model behavior; stitching preserves learned dynamics but requires more KV memory and complexity.
[06:19] Omar: Which is safer?
[06:20] Maya: Start with frequency rescaling as a compatibility test (low risk), then if you need more fidelity do stitching with careful fine-tune on extended contexts. We'll provide a validation harness.
[06:29] Jon: On the infra side: for on-prem we need to map GPU local KV memory across nodes for hotspot experts—do we want to colocate experts by routing affinity?
[06:38] Maya: Yes, expert placement matters. For heavy MoE use you should co-locate hot experts on the same host when possible. Our placement heuristic uses recent routing histograms to place top-k experts per tenant on the same rack to minimize cross-host packet movement. For on-prem, we can expose placement hints to your scheduler (nomad/k8s) via the Redwood agent.
[06:57] Dina: Network-wise we'll need low latency RDMA or at least 10Gb with tuned TCP. Can Redwood run with TLS over RDMA?
[07:05] Jon: For private deployments we support mTLS for control plane and optional in-cluster encryption for data plane. RDMA is supported by the runtime on systems with IB; we fallback to optimized TCP with kernel tuning. We'll share the perf delta matrix.
[07:19] Alex: Quick demo of a trace—Maya pulls up a live trace (shared) showing an MoE burst where routing hash distribution was skewed and caused three experts to spike.
[07:28] Maya: See this region, p99 CPU wait goes up while GPU remains underutilized because dispatch created micro-fragments—this is fixed by multiplexed routing. Notice KV miss rate spikes aligned with new session starts.
[07:41] Chris: For the multiplex window size, what do you recommend for 250ms p99 SLO?
[07:46] Maya: Start at 20ms windows with an adaptive limiter: if queue depth is low or latency approaches SLO, reduce the window. We'll show the config: window_ms=20; max_delay_ms=40; adaptive=true. It typically keeps p99 within bounds for mixed workloads.
[08:00] Omar: Any special logging we should enable for debugging expert skew?
[08:03] Maya: Yes—enable routing_histogram, kv_hit_rate_by_prefix, and expert_backpressure counters at DEBUG level for a short trial window. Those logs are lightweight but very informative.
[08:13] Dina: On security/compliance—can we get the SOC2 and encryption at rest details?
[08:16] Alex: We'll send the security one-pager; Redwood Private supports customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) and audit logs. For on-prem we give you the full control plane image and we can run the attestation steps.
[08:28] Chris: Last part—billing and cost predictability. If we use multiplexed routing and caching, what's the expected unit cost delta?
[08:35] Maya: Benchmarks show on heavy MoE mix you can reduce per-token GPU time by ~20-35% vs naive routing. With caching (good warm hit rates) you can reduce inference cost further because many tokens are prefix-only and served from cache primitives. We'll provide the benchmark spreadsheet by tomorrow.
[08:49] Alex: Alright let's capture concrete next steps and action items.
[08:53] Chris: Thanks, this was very helpful.

Endnotes / rough timestamps aligned:
- 00:00–01:20: context and infra constraints (NAT/keepalive)
- 01:20–05:50: routing, multiplexing, and quantization strategies
- 05:50–07:05: RoPE scaling and long-context strategies
- 07:05–08:35: deployment/placement, networking, and security
- 08:35–end: billing, benchmarks, next steps

Transcript quirks: occasional mis-transcriptions of parameter names (e.g., 'knob-20' instead of 'window_ms'), speaker overlaps, and truncated words noted in logs.
